title: The House of Al-Arqam
subtitle: The Secret Sanctuary, Quranic Study, and Community Formation
summary: The private phase of preaching in Makkah, the incident in the mountain passes, the gatherings at Dar al-Arqam near Mount Safa, night prayer and Qur'anic teaching, the brotherhood of the early believers, Ibn Mas'ud's public recitation, and an outline of the later conversions of Hamzah and Umar.

sections.text: The Clandestine Phase of Preaching

According to Ibn Ishaq, for about three years after revelation began, the mission proceeded privately, a phase later historians call al-Da'wah al-Sirriyyah (the private call). During this time the small community learned the revealed verses and strengthened its bonds before facing the open hostility of Quraysh.

At first the Companions prayed in small groups in the ravines around Makkah. Ibn Ishaq relates that while a group of them, including Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, was praying in a ravine, some polytheists of Quraysh came upon them, mocked them and began to fight them. Sa'd struck one of them with the jawbone of a camel and wounded him; Ibn Ishaq calls this the first blood shed in Islam.
Biographers connect incidents such as this with the use of a private house where the believers could meet, pray and learn in safety.
The Strategic Selection of Dar al-Arqam

That house belonged to al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam of the clan of Banu Makhzum, one of the early converts, who is reported to have been young at the time. Ibn Sa'd records that his house stood on al-Safa, near the sanctuary.

Later writers have suggested reasons why the house was suitable: al-Arqam belonged to Banu Makhzum rather than to the Prophet's own clan, and his conversion may not yet have been widely known. These are later interpretations rather than statements found in the early sources.
The slopes of Mount Safa near the sacred precinct where Dar al-Arqam provided sanctuary.
Spiritual Formation and Quranic Pedagogy

In the house of al-Arqam, the Prophet would meet his Companions, recite to them the verses as they were revealed and explain their meanings. The surahs of this period dwell on the majesty of God, the Resurrection, moral accountability and the stories of earlier prophets.

There the believers prayed together behind the Prophet and encouraged one another to remain patient. Their worship was not confined to these gatherings: the Qur'an itself describes the Prophet and a group of those with him standing in prayer for long portions of the night.

Commentators count Surah al-Muzzammil among the earliest revelations. Its opening verses command the Prophet to stand in prayer at night and recite the Qur'an slowly and distinctly, and its final verse acknowledges that he and a group of those with him had been standing nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it.

'O you who wraps himself, stand in prayer by night, except for a little; half of it, or a little less, or a little more, and recite the Qur'an with measured recitation.' — The Qur'an, Surah Al-Muzzammil 73:1–4
Eradication of Social Hierarchy

In the house of al-Arqam, men of different standing sat together. Wealthy Qurayshis such as 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and Abu Bakr sat with poorer converts, freedmen and foreigners such as Bilal the Abyssinian, Suhayb, known as al-Rumi, and Khabbab ibn al-Aratt.
There, honour was taught in terms of consciousness of God (taqwa) rather than tribe or wealth. The companionship formed in that house later helped the believers endure the persecution that followed.

As the community grew, some of its members began to show their faith more openly. Ibn Ishaq relates that the Companions remarked that Quraysh had never heard the Qur'an recited aloud to them, and that 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud offered to do it. They feared for him, since he had no clan to protect him, but he went to the sanctuary in the forenoon and recited aloud the opening of Surah al-Rahman. Quraysh rose and struck him in the face, and he returned to his companions bearing the marks of the blows, saying that he was ready to do it again. Later compilers count him as the first after the Prophet to recite the Qur'an aloud in Makkah.
The quiet alleys of Makkah where early believers gathered under cover of night.
The Pivotal Accessions of Hamzah and Umar

Two conversions would later change the position of the believers in Makkah. Many biographers place them in the sixth year of prophethood, after the first emigration to Abyssinia described in a later chapter, though some place them earlier. Ibn Ishaq relates that Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's uncle and a renowned hunter, heard that Abu Jahl had insulted his nephew, struck Abu Jahl with his bow, and declared that he followed Muhammad's religion. The reports differ over whether he then came to the Prophet in the house of al-Arqam.

Shortly after Hamzah, according to many accounts, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab accepted Islam. Al-Tirmidhi records the Prophet's prayer: 'O God, strengthen Islam through whichever of these two men is more beloved to You: Abu Jahl or 'Umar ibn al-Khattab,' adding that 'Umar was the more beloved of the two to him. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said, in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari: 'We have been strong since 'Umar accepted Islam.' The story of 'Umar's conversion is told in a later chapter.
The house of al-Arqam remained, in later memory, the first place where this small community met, learned the Qur'an and prayed together before the call became public.
